claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, its SystemOne model, within the past week relative to the post's publication (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (called 'noul') questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are 'the perfect complement to agentic work.'
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.
GeoDeploy pairs Jev's confidence-scored decisions with the Pulumi Automation API to place and scale Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, and gates every AI decision on confidence.
GeoDeploy is released as open source.
GeoDeploy's deployment request lets you specify target geos with traffic share and a data-residency rule (EU-only, US-only, or in-country).
GeoDeploy's deployment request takes a container image and the platforms it's built for (amd64, arm64, or both).
GeoDeploy's deployment request takes a workload shape (replicas, CPU and memory per pod, egress, storage) and constraints (allowed providers, max number of providers, budget).
In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing, does all the math, and never makes judgment calls.
In GeoDeploy, Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use, and never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names.
In GeoDeploy, Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS, and never decides anything.
GeoDeploy maps each business region (geo) to a canonical location and residency class.
GeoDeploy lists every region with managed Kubernetes and uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy uses plain, deterministic TypeScript to bin-pack pods onto nodes, filter out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and compute a monthly cost for each candidate region.
In GeoDeploy, Jev picks the winning region and modules for each geo.

GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules covering EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy will not run the provisioning step unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
The link target /automation/ exists as a Pulumi Automation API page.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a `plan.json` and `plan.md` containing the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Unlike a general-purpose LLM, Jev doesn't return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence.
Jev returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives: choice(), score(), and noul().
Jev's `choice()` primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's `score()` primitive rates something against a rubric you describe.
GeoDeploy's score rubrics use 10 levels.
Jev's `noul()` primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Jev only ever selects from closed sets in GeoDeploy, choosing among region IDs that GeoDeploy has already priced and checked.
Because Jev selects only from a closed list, a hallucinated region such as `us-west-9` or a made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates, along with the constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.

In one call per geo, GeoDeploy asks Jev for a region selection (choice), five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard yes/no checks (data residency satisfied, enough capacity), and a fallback backup region (choice).
GeoDeploy's Jev question definitions live in `packages/decide/src/questions.ts`.
The `@typesafe-ai/sdk` package exports `choice`, `noul`, and `score` functions.

In the TypeSafe SDK, `choice(prompt, options)` takes a question string and options, `score(prompt, levels)` takes a question and rubric levels, and `noul(prompt, {true, false})` takes a question and descriptions for the true and false outcomes.
The options passed to `choice()` in GeoDeploy are the priced candidates themselves, keyed by ID, so Jev cannot answer with a region that isn't on the list.
TypeSafe's advice for writing rubrics is to 'describe situations, not degrees.'

GeoDeploy's coverage rubric levels run from 'Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence' up to 'In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center.'

The TypeSafe SDK exposes a `TypeSafeClient` class whose `systemOne({ state, questions })` method returns a result with an `answers` object (e.g. `a.selection.choice`, `a.selection.confidence`, `a.residencyOk.noul`, `a.coverage.score`).
GeoDeploy sends the whole question set to Jev in one call, along with the state Jev reasons over.
GeoDeploy's five scores feed a ranking system with weight profiles: latency-optimized (the default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because GeoDeploy's ranking weights live in code, the ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy's WEIGHT_PROFILES define latency-optimized as cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12; balanced as 0.25/0.25/0.2/0.12/0.18; residency-first as 0.12/0.12/0.38/0.23/0.15; failure-domain as 0.08/0.17/0.48/0.15/0.12.
In GeoDeploy's composite ranking, sprawl risk is subtracted from the score rather than added.
Every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), so Jev decides only ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.
In GeoDeploy, a data-residency answer with confidence below 0.95 is a hard reject.
In GeoDeploy, a region choice for a new cluster requires 0.90 confidence; if it doesn't pass, the top three candidates are flagged for a human to choose.
In GeoDeploy, a region choice when a stack already exists requires 0.75 confidence; if it doesn't pass, the existing region is kept.
In GeoDeploy, an ingress or autoscaling module choice requires 0.85 confidence; if it doesn't pass, the registry default is used.
In GeoDeploy, a node-pool sizing tier choice requires 0.60 confidence; if it doesn't pass, the bin-packing result is used.
In GeoDeploy, region pick, residency, and capacity answers have a global confidence floor of 0.50; below it the AI path is dropped for that geo.
The residency gate check shown is from `packages/decide/src/engine.ts` in GeoDeploy, followed by a validation that the selection is one of the candidates.
Enforcing a confidence gate in GeoDeploy is plain deterministic code, not model-driven.
Each `AiPathAborted` error in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so even a rejected answer ends up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or returns an error, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing the residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.
Self-driving mode in GeoDeploy is enabled with `geodeploy monitor`.

In self-driving mode, GeoDeploy periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with the answers `no-change`, `scale-up:<geo>`, `scale-down:<geo>`, or `shift:<from>-><to>`, plus a separate check on disruption risk.
In self-driving mode, code (not Jev) computes the actual node-count changes.
In GeoDeploy self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically.
In GeoDeploy self-driving mode, between 0.70 and 0.85 confidence the resize is suggested for a human to approve.
In GeoDeploy self-driving mode, below 0.70 confidence GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.

CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency, error rates, or application-specific metrics once a traffic baseline is established.
To get started with GeoDeploy you need access to Jev and a cloud provider.
The GitHub repository pulumi/devx-geodeploy exists and hosts GeoDeploy.
The page /docs/iac/automation-api/ exists as the Pulumi Automation API docs.
https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction exists as the TypeSafe Jev docs.
